# Table Structure and Freshness {#sec-table-validations}

```{python}
#| include: false
import pointblank as pb
pb.config(report_incl_header=False, report_incl_footer=False)
```


Column checks look at values and row checks look at records, but both assume you have the right
table in front of you. Table-level checks test that assumption. They ask whether the table has the
columns you expect, whether it holds a plausible amount of data, whether it is recent enough to
trust, and whether it matches another table you are comparing it against. If any of these is off,
the results of the other checks in a plan may not mean much.

The problems these checks catch tend to cause confusing failures further down the line. For
example, a column that gets renamed upstream can make downstream queries fail or quietly return
nulls, and a feed that stops updating keeps serving old numbers that still look perfectly valid.
These are problems with the table itself rather than with individual values, so it helps to check
for them directly instead of trying to work backward from a pile of value-level failures.

We use the `game_revenue` dataset for the structural checks and small hand-built tables where a
self-contained example is clearer.

```{python}
game_revenue = pb.load_dataset(dataset="game_revenue", tbl_type="polars")
```

We start with the most basic structural question: are the columns you expect actually there?

## Schema validation

Pipeline code makes assumptions about a table's structure. It expects certain columns to exist,
with certain names and certain types. When one of those assumptions breaks, the pipeline usually
breaks too. Schema validation writes those assumptions down so that a violation is caught as soon
as the data arrives.

### Checking that columns exist

The `col_exists()` method is the simplest structural check. It confirms that the named columns are
present, and each column gets its own test unit.

```{python}
(
    pb.Validate(data=game_revenue)
    .col_exists(columns=["player_id", "session_id", "item_type", "item_revenue"])
    .interrogate()
)
```

All four columns are present, so all four steps pass. Since each column is its own step, a missing
column shows up on its own row in the report. Let's ask for a column that does not exist.

```{python}
(
    pb.Validate(data=game_revenue)
    .col_exists(columns=["player_id", "customer_id"])
    .interrogate()
)
```

The `player_id` step passes and the `customer_id` step fails, which tells you exactly which column
is missing. This is often the first thing to check on a table you are not familiar with or that
someone else maintains, since everything else depends on the columns being there.

### Matching names and types

Usually you care about types as well as names, and sometimes about column order too. The
`col_schema_match()` method checks a table against a `Schema`, an object that lists the column names
and types you expect. A schema can list every column in order, which is the strictest check. In
practice, you often list only the columns you depend on and relax the match so that extra columns
and a different order are allowed.

```{python}
schema = pb.Schema(columns=[("player_id", "String"), ("item_revenue", "Float64")])

(
    pb.Validate(data=game_revenue)
    .col_schema_match(schema=schema, complete=False, in_order=False)
    .interrogate()
)
```

The single test unit passes, because both columns exist with the stated types. Setting
`complete=False` allows the table to have columns that are not in the schema, and `in_order=False`
allows the columns to appear in any order. Together they say "these columns must exist with these
types" without requiring them to be the only columns or to appear in this order. Next, let's claim
that `player_id` is an integer when it is actually a string.

```{python}
(
    pb.Validate(data=game_revenue)
    .col_schema_match(
        schema=pb.Schema(columns=[("player_id", "Int64")]),
        complete=False,
        in_order=False,
    )
    .interrogate()
)
```

The check fails because the declared type does not match the actual one. It is much easier to find
out about a type change here than through a confusing error later in your analysis.

### Tightening or relaxing the match

By default the match is strict. The schema has to list every column, in order, with exactly matching
names and types. (Our two-column schema from above would fail with the defaults, because
`game_revenue` has eleven columns.) Several arguments relax these requirements one at a time. It is
worth seeing each of them, because the right setting can decide whether a plan survives a harmless
change in how the data is produced. First, column order. Here is a schema that lists two columns in
the opposite order from the table, with order enforced.

```{python}
schema = pb.Schema(columns=[("item_revenue", "Float64"), ("player_id", "String")])

(
    pb.Validate(data=game_revenue)
    .col_schema_match(schema=schema, complete=False, in_order=True)
    .interrogate()
)
```

The check fails, because `item_revenue` comes after `player_id` in the table. Setting
`in_order=False` accepts the columns in any position.

```{python}
(
    pb.Validate(data=game_revenue)
    .col_schema_match(schema=schema, complete=False, in_order=False)
    .interrogate()
)
```

Now it passes. Type matching can be relaxed as well. With `case_sensitive_dtypes=False` and
`full_match_dtypes=False`, a type name can differ in case and can be a partial match. So declaring
`player_id` as `"string"` matches its actual `String` type.

```{python}
(
    pb.Validate(data=game_revenue)
    .col_schema_match(
        schema=pb.Schema(columns=[("player_id", "string")]),
        complete=False, in_order=False,
        case_sensitive_dtypes=False, full_match_dtypes=False,
    )
    .interrogate()
)
```

This passes. Without those two arguments, the same schema fails, because `"string"` and `"String"`
are not an exact match. The relaxed settings help when different systems spell the same type
differently, such as `int64` and `Int64`. If a column can legitimately arrive as one of several
types, you can list all of them, and the match passes if the actual type is any one of those.

```{python}
(
    pb.Validate(data=game_revenue)
    .col_schema_match(
        schema=pb.Schema(columns=[("item_revenue", ["Float64", "Float32"])]),
        complete=False, in_order=False,
    )
    .interrogate()
)
```

This passes because `item_revenue` is `Float64`, which is one of the listed types. If you only care
that a column exists and not what type it has, you can list it without a type.

```{python}
(
    pb.Validate(data=game_revenue)
    .col_schema_match(
        schema=pb.Schema(columns=[("player_id",), ("item_type",)]),
        complete=False, in_order=False,
    )
    .interrogate()
)
```

That passes because both columns are present. When choosing among these options, think about which
parts of the structure your code actually depends on. A good rule is to use the loosest setting that
still catches the changes you are worried about.

## Dimensional validation

A table can have exactly the right schema and still hold the wrong amount of data. A load that only
captured half the records is one example, and a schema check will not notice it. Checking the
table's dimensions can.

### Row counts


### Column counts

The `col_count_match()` method does the same thing for the number of columns. The `game_revenue`
table has 11.

```{python}
(
    pb.Validate(data=game_revenue)
    .col_count_match(count=11)
    .interrogate()
)
```

The check passes. A column count is an easy way to notice that a table gained or lost columns
between runs, which could otherwise go unnoticed as long as the columns your code reads are still
there. Like `row_count_match()`, it accepts `inverse=True` to require any count other than the one
given.

## Table comparison

Sometimes the question is whether a table matches another table exactly. The `tbl_match()` method
compares a table against a reference in stages, each stricter than the last. It checks the column
count, then the row count, then the schema, and finally the values cell by cell, and it fails at the
first stage where the tables differ. The whole comparison produces a single test unit. Two identical
tables pass.
